newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Nicolas Cage asks, Where are the heroes?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Nicolas Cage asks, Where are the heroes?.

text.p: Oscar-winner Nicolas Cage is a man on a mission. After years of playing oddballs, weirdos and just plain freaks, he wants to bring heroism and honour back to the movies.

His transformation will be revealed next year when he plays that paragon of right, Superman, but with a uniquely 90's twist. Cage's "Man of Steel" will be a sensitive, caring guy who helps people because deep down he needs to be loved.

"Superman to me is an American myth. The English have Shakespeare, the Greeks have Zeus, Americans have Superman and Batman," he said. "I decided to do something responsible and positive and different with it."

His appearance as Clark Kent's alter ego in Tim Burton's movie next year will be as "a beautiful freak ... needing to do heroic acts so people would like him," Cage said. "I want to redefine the whole meaning of Superman going into a new millennium. I want to utilize his feelings of being different, of being alien, and make that kid in school think twice about teasing that weird kid."

Although Cage will not be donning the cape and tights of Superman until next year, this summer he takes a step on the road to heroic hero in "Con Air," an action movie about a bunch of hardened convicts who hijack a plane. In the film, opening in the United States on June 6 and also starring John Malkovich and John Cusack, Cage plays an Army Ranger jailed for killing a man who insulted his uniform and his wife.

Cage, who is on a government plane transporting prisoners in the film because he has been freed and is going home to his wife and daughter, plays it like a modern-day Odysseus as the hijack tests his sense of honour and morality.
WANTS GOOD GUYS BACK IN FILMS

In an interview, he decried the decline of such qualities on screen. "There's a level of cynicism you have to get past for the character to show a sense of morality and not to run away from his best friend," he told Reuters.
"The biggest issue is how to make it believable. I would like to believe that the man is out there and that when the chips are down he does the right thing."

In the movie magazine Premiere, which recently dubbed him "Hollywood's Prince of Darkness," Cage expanded on the theme of honour. "Movies like 'High Noon' were once acceptable -- that sort of code of honour that makes a man stop his wedding day and do the right thing."

But Cage may find it difficult getting fans to accept his metamorphosis into Gary Cooper or John Wayne, given the roles he has played in a 15-year Hollywood career. Known as one of Hollywood's more intense actors, he made his debut in 1983 in his uncle Francis Ford Coppola's "Rumble Fish" under his real name of Nicolas Coppola.

After changing his name to Cage, he was in two more Coppola films, "The Cotton Club" and "Peggy Sue Got Married." He was an orange-haired street punk in "Valley Girl," a one-handed baker wooing Cher in "Moonstruck," a nutty bloodsucker in "Vampire's Kiss" and a violent vagabond in "Wild at Heart."
WON FAME PLAYING A DRUNK
His best actor Oscar-winning role last year in "Leaving Las Vegas" was as a suicidal alcoholic writer.

He turned down a part in "Top Gun" because he objected to the military action film's rightwing message. And his aura of enigma is heightened by a menacing tattoo of a lizard on his shoulder -- but the lizard is wearing a top hat.
Following last year's "The Rock," he made two more action films, "Con Air" and "Face/Off" with John Travolta, but he vowed that's it for "Nick Cage - Action Hero."
"This is my double album but my last (action roles) for a while," he said. "It allowed me to master a genre, but now with this I've done all I can with action movies.
"Certain movies have obviously to entertain -- that's fair and cogent. Other movies should be more thought-provoking and introspective and not necessarily just to entertain."
Marriage to actress Patricia Arquette and having a 6-year-old son, Weston, by former girlfriend Christina Fulton, may have mellowed Cage somewhat.

"Life's experience always affects my work and makes me more sensitive to everything," he said. "Fatherhood has changed me. Now I am interested in more theatrical kinds of characters. I feel inspiration from a sense of security and happiness."
